'''Jed Hoyer''' (born December 7, 1973) is an American sports executive who is the [[president of baseball operations]] for the [[Chicago Cubs]] of [[Major League Baseball]] (MLB).<ref name=autogenerated1>{{cite web|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/2011-10-27/hoyer-mcleod-leave-san-diego-padres-join-theo-epstein-with-chicago-cubs.html|title=Hoyer, McLeod Leave San Diego Padres, Join Theo Epstein With Chicago Cubs|date=October 27, 2011|last=Kercheval| first=Nancy| work=Bloomberg| access-date=March 22, 2021}}</ref> He has been the general manager of the [[San Diego Padres]] and the assistant general manager of the [[Boston Red Sox]].

==Early and personal life==
Hoyer was born in [[Plymouth, New Hampshire]], and is Jewish.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=CRhSDgAAQBAJ&dq=jed+hoyer+born&pg=PT92 ''Plan: Epstein, Maddon, and the Audacious Blueprint for a Cubs Dynasty'' - David Kaplan, Anthony Rizzo, Bud Selig<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref><ref>[http://www.cjnews.com/culture/sports/jewish-players-sportspeople-looking-dominate-2015-mlb-playoffs "Here are the Jewish players and sportspeople looking to dominate the 2015 MLB playoffs" - ''The Canadian Jewish News''<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref><ref>[https://www.jta.org/2016/10/26/life-religion/theo-epstein-vs-mike-chernoff-the-jewish-minds-behind-the-cubs-and-the-indians "Theo Epstein vs. Mike Chernoff: The Jewish minds behind the Cubs and the Indians"] | [[Jewish Telegraphic Agency]]<!-- Bot generated title --></ref>

Hoyer graduated from the [[Holderness School]] in [[Holderness, New Hampshire]], where his mother was the school nurse and his father was the school doctor, in 1992.<ref>[https://www.holderness.org/page/news-detail?pk=886719 "Chicago Cubs General Manager Jed Hoyer ’92 to Speak at Commencement"<!-- Bot generated title -->]{{Dead link|date=October 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref><ref>[http://www.thebaseballcube.com/players/profile.asp?ID=160558 "Jed Hoyer" - The Baseball Cube<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref> He then went to [[Wesleyan University]] in Connecticut, majoring in American history, where he was a shortstop and star pitcher who shares Wesleyan's career saves record with Sam Elias and Nick Miceli.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://athletics.wesleyan.edu/sports/bsb/team_records |title="Selected All-Time Offensive and Pitching Records" - Wesleyan Athletics<!-- Bot generated title --> |access-date=October 12, 2016 |archive-date=October 12, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161012151002/http://athletics.wesleyan.edu/sports/bsb/team_records |url-status=dead }}</ref> During his time at Wesleyan University he was also initiated into and is a brother of [[Delta Kappa Epsilon]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.dke.org/this-week-in-dke-history/2014/10/27/this-week-in-dke-history-october-25th-october-31st |title=DKE {{!}} Delta Kappa Epsilon<!-- Bot generated title --> |access-date=December 17, 2016 |archive-date=December 21, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161221024945/http://www.dke.org/this-week-in-dke-history/2014/10/27/this-week-in-dke-history-october-25th-october-31st |url-status=dead }}</ref> In 1995, he played [[collegiate summer baseball]] with the [[Bourne Braves]] of the [[Cape Cod Baseball League]],<ref>{{cite web|author=Joe Pelletier |url=https://www.nhregister.com/news/article/WESLEYAN-FOOTPRINTS-Jed-Hoyer-96-was-star-on-11489673.php |title=Wesleyan Footprints: Jed Hoyer '96 was star on and off baseball field |publisher=New Haven Register |date=September 3, 2012 |accessdate=July 20, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|author=Melissa Isaacson |url=https://www.espn.com/chicago/mlb/story/_/id/7156063/jed-hoyer-path-chicago-cubs-general-manager-swift-unconventional |title=New Cubs GM Hoyer took unique path |work=espn.com |date=October 27, 2011 |accessdate=July 20, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|author= |url=https://athletics.wesleyan.edu/sports/2020/8/20/wesleyan-baseball-in-the-pros.aspx |title=Wesleyan Baseball in the Cape Cod League |publisher=wesleyan.edu |date= |accessdate=July 20, 2021}}</ref> and the Waterbury Barons of the [[New England Collegiate Baseball League]], seeing innings on the mound and at shortstop. Hoyer worked in the admissions office and then the alumni/development office, and was also a baseball coach at the university after graduating. He worked in the admissions department of [[Kenyon College]] before joining the Red Sox at 28.<ref name=Isaacson>{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/chicago/mlb/story/_/id/7156063/jed-hoyer-path-chicago-cubs-general-manager-swift-unconventional|title=He was going to be GM someday|date=October 27, 2011|last=Isaacson| first=Melissa| work=ESPN|access-date=March 22, 2021}}</ref>

He married Merrill Muckerman in June 2010 in St. Louis.

==Baseball career==
He joined the Red Sox in 2002, after the ownership of [[John W. Henry]], [[Tom Werner]], and [[Larry Lucchino]] took over the team from [[John Harrington (Red Sox CEO)|John Harrington]]. He worked as assistant to the general manager until December 2005. He then was given the title of assistant general manager. Hoyer briefly served as co-general manager of the Red Sox from December 12, 2005, to January 19, 2006, and then returning to his previous job of assistant general manager. In November 2003, he accompanied general manager [[Theo Epstein]] to [[Arizona]] to persuade pitcher [[Curt Schilling]] to accept a trade to the Red Sox, spending [[Thanksgiving]] at Schilling's home in what was eventually a successful effort.<ref name=Isaacson/>

===Boston Red Sox===
When Epstein left his position on October 31, 2005, Hoyer was part of a group of four executives, called the "Gang of Four", that kept the club running in Epstein's absence. Other members of the "gang" were [[Ben Cherington]], [[Bill Lajoie]], and [[Craig Shipley]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://archive.boston.com/sports/baseball/redsox/articles/2005/11/09/antonetti_added_to_sox_list/|title=Boston Red Sox - Antonetti added to Sox' list |date=November 9, 2005| last=Edes| first=Gordon |work=The Boston Globe|access-date=March 22, 2021}}</ref> a group which completed trades for, among others, [[Josh Beckett]], [[Mike Lowell]], [[Mark Loretta]], and [[Andy Marte]]. Shortly after the winter meetings were completed in early December, Hoyer and Cherington were promoted to co-general managers, where they remained until Epstein returned to his original position on January 19, 2006, after a 10-week hiatus.<ref name=Isaacson/> Hoyer was also a key player in decision-making regarding players and their contracts. Beginning in 2008, he became the first "Resident Expert" for the Fenway neighborhood on [https://web.archive.org/web/20080705135547/http://www.povo.com/ Povo.com], a local wiki whose platform lets one share their insider's knowledge of Boston.

Following the 2007 season, Hoyer interviewed to become general manager of the [[Pittsburgh Pirates]], a job that went to [[Neal Huntington]] of the [[Cleveland Indians]] organization.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://blogs.unionleader.com/gray/?m=200709 |title=Kevin Gray » 2007 » September |access-date=September 18, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090425064643/http://blogs.unionleader.com/gray/?m=200709 |archive-date=April 25, 2009 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Similarly, during the 2009 season, Hoyer interviewed to become the GM of the [[Washington Nationals]], who appointed their own assistant GM, [[Mike Rizzo (baseball)|Mike Rizzo]], to the top spot.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2009/08/11/AR2009081103045.html|title=Rizzo Among Three Primary Candidates for Permanent GM Job|date=August 12, 2009|last=Harlan| first=Chico| newspaper=Washington Post| access-date=March 22, 2021}}</ref>

===San Diego Padres===
[[File:Jed Hoyer 2011.jpg|thumb|180px|Jed Hoyer in 2011]]
In October 2009 he was hired as the [[San Diego Padres]]' general manager.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://mlb.mlb.com/news/article.jsp?ymd=20091026&content_id=7555176&vkey=news_mlb&fext=.jsp&c_id=mlb|title=Padres name Hoyer as new GM|work=Major League Baseball|access-date=October 8, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www3.signonsandiego.com/stories/2009/oct/26/n115416-padres-sullivan26/?padres|title=Friend thinks the fix is in for detail-driven Hoyer|work=U-T San Diego|access-date=October 8, 2014|archive-date=October 31, 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091031023549/http://www3.signonsandiego.com/stories/2009/oct/26/n115416-padres-sullivan26/?padres|url-status=dead}}</ref> Perhaps his best known deal as GM of the Padres was when he sent 1B [[Adrián González]] to the Red Sox in exchange for RHP [[Casey Kelly]], OF [[Reymond Fuentes]], utility man [[Eric Patterson (baseball)|Eric Patterson]], and 1B [[Anthony Rizzo (baseball)|Anthony Rizzo]].

===Chicago Cubs===
On October 26, 2011, the [[Chicago Cubs]] announced that Jed Hoyer and Jason McLeod had joined the club. Hoyer became the general manager, while McLeod would work in the scouting department.<ref name=autogenerated1 /> The Cubs announced that compensation for Hoyer would be worked out before the [[Rule 5 Draft]].

In September 2016 the Cubs signed him to a five-year contract through 2021.<ref>{{Cite web|url= http://www.chicagotribune.com/sports/baseball/cubs/ct-cubs-jed-hoyer-jason-mcleod-2021-20160930-story.html |title=Cubs' Jed Hoyer, Jason McLeod receive extensions through 2021 |date=September 30, 2016|last=Gonzalez |first=Mark |access-date=March 22, 2021|work=Chicago Tribune}}</ref> On November 17, 2020, the Cubs named Hoyer president of baseball operations, taking over following Epstein's resignation. He signed another five-year deal in November 2020, running through 2025.<ref>{{cite web |title=Chicago Cubs president Jed Hoyer gets five-year contract |url=https://www.espn.com/mlb/story/_/id/30374362/chicago-cubs-president-jed-hoyer-gets-five-year-contract |website=espn.com |date=November 23, 2020 |publisher=ESPN, Inc. |access-date=5 December 2021}}</ref> On July 29, 2025, Hoyer and the Cubs reached another contract extension.<ref>{{cite news |title=Cubs reach multiyear extension with president of baseball ops Jed Hoyer |url=https://www.espn.com/mlb/story/_/id/45844965/cubs-reach-multiyear-extension-president-baseball-ops-jed-hoyer |access-date=July 29, 2025 |date=July 29, 2025}}</ref>
